title: Console walkthrough - Usage analytics & per-route cost breakdown (Hyperion Retail)
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Hyperion through the Console usage analytics, per-route dashboards, and cost breakdown. Key topics: per-route token cost, model pinning, batching recommendations, and compliance concerns for PII in logs. Agreed next steps: share benchmark spreadsheet, security pack, and schedule pilot baseline run.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-01
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen, Maya Lopez (Redwood); Jordan Meyers, Priya Rao, Ethan Brooks, Lina Gomez (Hyperion)

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'll hand it over to Maya to do a quick Console walkthrough, focusing on usage analytics and per-route cost breakdown - this is the page customers use to understand unit economics.
[00:10] Maya (Redwood SE): Great thanks Alex. Hi Jordan, Priya - quick confirm, are you looking for per-route cost to attribute to business units, or more on model-level pricing?
[00:18] Jordan (Hyperion CTO): Primarily per-route so product teams can see cost by feature, but model-level is also useful for the infra team.
[00:25] Maya: Perfect. I'm sharing my screen - go to Console > Analytics > Routes. You can see top panel, total tokens, avg latency, errors. Note the timeframe selector at top-right.
[00:40] Priya: Quick Q - how accurate is the token accounting? We need it to match billing to the cent for internal chargebacks.
[00:49] Maya: Good question. We compute tokens based on the model tokenizer heuristics and our runtime's tokenization. There's a small delta vs model vendor billing sometimes due to rounding and streaming chunks; usually within 0.5-1% per month. We also provide raw token logs per request if you need exact reconciliation.
[01:05] Ethan: So we could ingest those logs into our finops pipeline?
[01:08] Maya: Yeah, you can export CSV or push to S3 monthly, or use our API to pull per-route usage programmatically.
[01:14] Lina: Are those exports PII-safe? We don't want prompt text in logs.
[01:19] Maya: By default we store metadata only (token counts, latencies, model id). Full request/response logging is opt-in and can be redacted; we have redaction hooks and KMS support - Alex can send the security pack with our redaction and retention controls.
[01:33] Alex: Yep I'll drop the security docs.
[01:35] Maya: Back to the dashboard - scroll down to the per-route table. Each route shows tokens in, tokens out, avg tokens per call, avg latency, cost per 1k tokens, and total cost.
[01:47] Jordan: That cost per 1k tokens - is that based on our plan or on public hosted pricing?
[01:52] Maya: It uses your effective rate. For hosted evals it's the public catalog price; for Dedicated/Reserved it's based on provisioned capacity and your committed unit economics - we show both nominal and amortized cost.
[02:06] Priya: Amortized? explain that a bit.
[02:09] Maya: Sure. Nominal is the per-token runtime cost. Amortized factors in reserved GPU cost divided across estimated token throughput and includes infra overhead like replication and caching. It's meant to show the practical unit economics if you buy dedicated capacity.
[02:26] Ethan: Does the console surface batching/caching effects?
[02:30] Maya: Yes - we have toggles to simulate different batching policies. In the route details pane you can run a 'what-if' that applies suggested batching and kv-prefix caching and shows expected token reduction and latency change.
[02:43] Priya: Hmm can it show impact on tail latency? Our SLA cares about p99.
[02:47] Maya: We show p50/p90/p99 latency distributions per route over the selected window. When you toggle batching, we overlay projected p99 based on observed sequence length distributions. It's an estimate but proven close in our benchmarks.
[02:59] [00:03:00] Jordan: I like that. For our POC we need a baseline run against our dataset. How do we pin a model version for the test?
[03:06] Maya: In the route config you can pin model version or set a rollout policy. We'll also support automatic fallback to lighter quantized variants. For the POC we recommend pinning to the exact model and quantization profile so the comparison is apples-to-apples.
[03:19] Alex: I'll include the recommended config in the follow-up.
[03:22] Priya: Any sample numbers you can share now for e.g., 8k context with batching?
[03:26] Maya: For reference, our internal benchmark: for 8k seq on A100-style fleet with continuous batching and kv caching we typically see 20-40% token cost reduction vs naive single-request execution depending on request similarity. But that varies with your prompt distribution.
[03:45] Ethan: Do you support per-route quotas and cost alerts?
[03:48] Maya: Yes alerts can be set for token spend, rate, and p99 latency per route. You can route alerts to Slack, PagerDuty, or webhooks.
[03:56] [00:04:00] Jordan: Ok, show me the cost breakdown for a sample route.
[04:00] Maya: Opening Route: "search-assist-frontend" - here we see tokens in 1.2M for the month, tokens out 3.5M, avg tokens in 120, avg latency 320ms, nominal cost $0.0026 per 1k tokens, amortized cost $0.0048 per 1k tokens, total cost $18.4k. We break down cost into model compute, infra amortization, and ops overhead.
[04:24] Priya: That ops overhead line - what's that include?
[04:27] Maya: things like orchestration, warmup buffers, telemetry retention, and licensing. We show a transparency tab that itemizes those components.
[04:36] Lina: Can we attribute costs to teams automatically? We have multiple product routes that map to org units.
[04:40] Maya: Absolutely - you can tag routes with cost center tags and generate per-team billing exports. There's also a per-route annotation API for programmatic tagging.
[04:49] Jordan: Competitors offer simpler per-model dashboards - how is Redwood different?
[04:53] Alex: The difference is the per-route view that ties runtime config to unit economics and operations signals. We add recommendations (batching, quantization) and show projected cost/latency tradeoffs side-by-side.
[05:05] [00:05:30] Priya: Security question again - where are these console logs stored? Region controls?
[05:10] Maya: For hosted we store analytics in regional buckets; you can choose EU/US/APAC. For Private/Dedicated, analytics can be pushed to your VPC or on-prem. Logs are encrypted with customer-managed keys if requested.
[05:21] Ethan: Any SOC2 or ISO certs?
[05:23] Alex: We are SOC2 Type II and have ISO 27001 in progress; full evidence is in the security pack I'll share.
[05:30] Priya: Great. For the POC timeline: we want a 2-week baseline ingest, then a 4-week pilot - is that realistic?
[05:38] Maya: Yes that's typical. Week 1 is integration and sample ingestion, week 2 baseline run, week 3-6 pilot with optimizations. We'll provide a runbook and sample metrics dashboard.
[05:49] Jordan: Pricing - can you show an example invoice or amortization calc?
[05:53] Maya: In the console there's an "estimate cost" modal that will compute monthly spend given traffic assumptions and reserved capacity options. We can export that as a spreadsheet.
[06:05] Alex: I'll send a sample amortization spreadsheet populated with the numbers we walked through today.
[06:08] [00:06:30] Priya: Talk to me about model fallbacks - if Dedicated capacity is saturated, can Redwood route to hosted lower-cost variant? We need graceful degradation.
[06:17] Maya: Yes, smart routing supports tiered fallbacks: dedicate pool -> regional hosted -> cheaper quantized variant. Fallbacks are policy-based and can be per-route.
[06:28] Lina: Will that preserve audit trails for requests that got routed?
[06:31] Maya: We retain request-level metadata regardless of routing; you can correlate request ids across backends. Full payloads are only stored if enabled.
[06:38] Jordan: Any gotchas on latency when failing over to hosted region? p99 will spike.
[06:42] Maya: Correct - fallback has higher network variance. In the routing modal you can set SLOs and automatic disable thresholds.
[06:50] [00:07:30] Ethan: For our finance team we need a monthly export with chargeback breakdown by route and cost center. Is that available today?
[06:57] Alex: Yes export is available and we can map routes to your GL codes. We'll also attach a sample ledger.
[07:03] Priya: For the baseline run we want token-level anonymization - remove PII in prompts before logs leave our network. How to implement?
[07:12] Maya: You can enable client-side redaction or use our redaction middleware which scrubs known patterns before logging. For extra safety we recommend client-side redaction plus server-side filters.
[07:22] [00:08:00] Jordan: Ok good. Any examples of customers that use per-route billing internally?
[07:26] Maya: Several retail customers do this to charge product teams. We can share an anonymized case study - I'll include it.
[07:32] Alex: I'll also share the onboarding checklist and recommended instance sizing for a pilot.
[07:35] Priya: What's the typical improvement you see after following the Optimize recommendations?
[07:41] Maya: On average customers see 25-35% cost reduction after enabling batching, caching, and model quantization policies, but again it's dependent on request shapes.
[07:52] [00:09:00] Jordan: Can you run a quick demo of the 'what-if' batching simulation on that search-assist route?
[09:04] Maya: Sure clicking into route -> Simulate -> choose batching strategy "continuous-batch-100ms". It runs a projection: projected tokens down 28%, p99 latency up 8%, estimated monthly cost down from $18.4k to $13.3k.
[09:20] Priya: Hmm p99 up 8% might violate our SLA, can the simulation show tradeoffs like reduce batching window to 50ms?
[09:27] Maya: Yes change window to 50ms: projected tokens down 18%, p99 up 2%, cost $15.1k. You can export the scenarios to compare.
[09:37] Ethan: Nice. How accurate are these projections historically?
[09:41] Maya: On our pilot customers we hit within 10-15% of projected cost and latency if the traffic pattern is stable; if you have bursty traffic it can diverge more. We always recommend a short controlled pilot.
[09:55] [00:10:00] Alex: Alright, let's recap and action items.
[10:03] Maya: Recap: shared Console routes view, per-route table, what-if batching, model pinning, exports, and security options.
[10:10] Priya: Next steps?
[10:12] Alex: I'll send: 1) security pack and SOC2 evidence, 2) amortization spreadsheet & sample invoice, 3) onboarding runbook and recommended pilot config, 4) a short checklist for redaction options.
[10:23] Maya: From SE side I'll share the benchmark spreadsheet and a suggested batching/caching config tailored to your seq length distribution. I'll also schedule a tech deep dive next week with your infra team to flesh out VPC networking.
[10:36] Jordan: Sounds good - let's schedule the POC kickoff for next Tuesday.
[10:40] Lina: One last Q - any blockers on us using customer-managed KMS for analytics encryption?
[10:45] Maya: No blockers, we support CMK via KMS. We'll document the steps.
[10:50] Alex: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[10:52] Jordan: Thanks all.

Transcript notes: occasional recognition errors ("kv cache" transcribed sometimes as "K V cache"), filler words, overlapping talk around 00:09-00:11.
